sysd-reliab-221.title: Packet forwarding in network load balancers
sysd-reliab-221.text: A network load balancer can hand a packet to its chosen backend in three ways. Network address translation needs a tracking-table entry for every connection, so it precludes a completely stateless fallback. Changing the destination MAC address lets the backend reply directly to the sender (Direct Server Response), which saves a great deal when replies are large. But every balancer and backend must then sit in one broadcast domain, which stops working at scale. Encapsulation wraps the packet in a GRE-encapsulated IP packet. Balancer and backend can then be on separate continents, at the price of 24 bytes of overhead that may exceed the MTU.

sysd-reliab-195.title: Managing expectations with SLOs
sysd-reliab-195.text: Publishing SLOs sets expectations for system behavior, so users can tell whether a service fits their use case. A team building a photo-sharing site might avoid a service promising strong durability and low cost for slightly lower availability, though it could suit an archival records system. Keeping an internal SLO tighter than the advertised one leaves room to respond to chronic problems before users see them. Do not overachieve either. Users build on what a service actually delivers, so performing far above its SLO breeds over-dependence. Remedies include planned outages, throttling some requests, or designs that are not faster under light load.

sysd-reliab-198.title: Request-based availability: counting requests instead of minutes
sysd-reliab-198.text: A system serving 2.5M requests a day with a 99.99% daily target can serve up to 250 errors and still meet it. That is request-based availability: the proportion of requests that succeed over a rolling window, instead of the proportion of time a system is up. Time-based availability counts uptime, and a 99.99% target allows up to 52.56 minutes of downtime a year. But for globally distributed services some traffic is almost always served somewhere, so uptime is rarely meaningful. The success rate over all requests approximates unplanned downtime as the end user sees it. Batch systems can count records processed successfully and unsuccessfully instead of requests.

sysd-reliab-199.title: Setting an availability target: what is one more nine worth?
sysd-reliab-199.text: One more nine of availability is worth what it adds in revenue. Raising a $1M-revenue service from 99.9% to 99.99% is worth $900, so ask whether that offsets the cost, which is often the key factor. A target also depends on what users expect, whether the service is paid or free, what competitors offer, and whether it serves consumers or enterprises. A fast-growing consumer product can take a lower target because feature speed matters more. Without a revenue translation, a yardstick is the background error rate of ISPs, between 0.01% and 1%. Errors driven below that fall within the noise of a user's Internet connection.

sysd-reliab-200.title: Multiple service levels for shared infrastructure
sysd-reliab-200.text: Clients of a shared storage system can want opposite things. Low-latency users want empty request queues, while offline-analysis users want queues never empty, so the system never idles. A cost-effective answer is to partition the infrastructure and offer it at multiple independent levels of service. Low-latency clusters carry substantial slack capacity for short queues and isolation. Throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy, perhaps at as little as 10-50% of the cost. Explicit levels expose the cost of each, so clients pick the cheapest that meets their needs. The classes can run on identical hardware and software, varying resource quantities, redundancy, geographic provisioning and configuration.

sysd-reliab-217.title: Borg: a cluster operating system that restarts failed tasks
sysd-reliab-217.text: Hardware failures are frequent: thousands of machines and thousands of disks fail in a typical cluster-year. Borg, a distributed cluster operating system, abstracts these failures away from users and service teams. It runs users' jobs, either long-running servers or batch processes, as sets of identical tasks on a cluster's machines. Borg finds machines for a job's tasks, monitors them, and kills and restarts a malfunctioning task, possibly on a different machine. Each job declares its resource needs, and Borg bin-packs tasks onto machines. Because tasks move, clients reach them through a naming service that resolves a name and task index to an IP address and port.

sysd-reliab-219.title: Life of a request through a large serving stack
sysd-reliab-219.text: A request to a large serving stack crosses many layers before the reply is assembled. It passes through DNS, a global load balancer and a reverse-proxy frontend, then application frontend and backend servers, and finally a storage layer such as Bigtable. The whole trip takes a few hundred milliseconds. GSLB, the global load balancer, steers the request at three points: the IP address returned to the user, the service frontend, and an unloaded backend. Many moving parts mean many potential points of failure, and a failing GSLB would wreak havoc. Rigorous testing, careful rollout and graceful degradation keep the service reliable.

sysd-reliab-218.title: N+2 capacity planning: spare tasks for updates and failures
sysd-reliab-218.text: Sizing a service divides expected peak load by what one task can handle, then adds spare tasks so peak load is still served during updates and machine failures. With about 100 QPS per task and an expected peak of about 3,470 QPS, at least 35 tasks are needed. N+2 raises this to 37, since an update plus a machine failure could otherwise leave only 35. Backends are placed per region, for example 17 tasks in the USA, 16 in Europe and 6 in Asia. South America uses 4 at N+1, saving 20% of hardware for a small risk of higher latency.

sysd-reliab-101.title: What a well-defined SLA contains
sysd-reliab-101.text: A well-defined SLA names the type of service and the performance level it expects, especially reliability and responsiveness. It describes how performance is monitored: which statistics are gathered, how often, and how customers can access them. It gives contact details and the order for reporting a problem. The response time frame is when the provider starts investigating, and the resolution time frame is when the issue is fixed. Finally, it states the repercussions. If the provider misses its commitments, the customer may have the right to terminate the contract or ask for a refund for losses from the service failure.

sysd-reliab-102.title: Cloud service level agreements
sysd-reliab-102.text: Because cloud resources are shared, a cloud SLA spans the cloud itself. Providers offer it as a service-based agreement rather than a customer-based one. Performance is measured and reported from the end user's ability to consume resources. Cloud SLAs focus on data center characteristics and, more recently, network characteristics to support end-to-end SLAs. The downside is that the complex environment makes the root cause of service interruptions hard to determine. Yet applications moved there must reach the same or more demanding service levels. Any SLA management strategy has two phases: negotiating the contract and monitoring its fulfillment in real time.

sysd-reliab-203.title: Black-box and white-box monitoring
sysd-reliab-203.text: Black-box monitoring tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it. White-box monitoring uses metrics exposed by the system's internals, such as logs or an HTTP handler emitting statistics. Black-box monitoring is symptom-oriented and catches active problems, so it suits paging: it only bothers a human when a problem is already causing real symptoms. White-box monitoring can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries, and it is essential for debugging. In a multilayered system one person's symptom is another's cause. Slow database reads are a symptom for the database SRE but a cause for the frontend SRE watching a slow website.

sysd-reliab-204.title: Alerting and paging: wake a human only when it matters
sysd-reliab-204.text: Paging a human is expensive, because it interrupts work or sleep. When pages are too frequent, people skim or ignore them, even a real one masked by noise, and outages can be prolonged. Good alerting therefore pages a human only for an urgent, actionable condition that is actively or imminently user-visible. Every page should be actionable, need intelligence rather than a robotic response, and concern a novel problem. People can react with urgency only a few times a day before becoming fatigued. Monitoring should answer what is broken (the symptom) and why (a possibly intermediate cause), and keeping the two apart is key. Put effort into catching symptoms rather than causes. Email alerts are of very limited value and quickly overrun with noise, so favor a dashboard of ongoing subcritical problems. Pages with rote responses are a red flag: remove the root cause or fully automate the response. In one over-alerting case, the team eased an SLO dominated by a long tail of mean latency to 75th percentile latency and disabled email alerts.

sysd-reliab-187.title: Incident management: from detection to post-incident review
sysd-reliab-187.text:
Left unmanaged, an incident can escalate into an emergency, crisis or disaster. Incident management is the process of limiting the disruption an incident could cause to operations, services or functions, followed by a return to business as usual. It identifies, analyzes and corrects hazards to prevent recurrence. An incident response or incident management team, designated beforehand or during the event, is put in control to restore normal functions, and an incident commander leads the response. Frameworks follow a lifecycle of detection, classification, response coordination, containment, recovery and post-incident review. In IT service management the first goal is restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible while minimizing business impact. Normal operation here means service within the SLA.

Afterward, post-incident analysis determines why the incident happened despite precautions. Its findings feed back into policy and its practical implementation. Root cause analysis should assess human factors. An active failure has immediate effects, while latent failures come from high-level decisions and lie dormant until a triggering event combines with them. Typical challenges are growing alert and event noise, a lengthy problem resolution process, and inability to predict and prevent service degradations or outages. For computer security incidents, a computer security incident response team analyzes the situation, determines how far an intrusion reached and takes corrective action.

sysd-reliab-105.title: SRE team models: five ways to organize
sysd-reliab-105.text: SRE teams are organized in several models: kitchen sink, infrastructure, product or application, embedded and consulting. A kitchen sink team oversees an expansive, often unbounded scope, including performance optimization, incident management and automation. Infrastructure teams keep the systems that support other teams' workflows up, fast and efficient, while platform teams develop the software and systems used across the organization. Product or application teams are dedicated to specific products, and large companies typically have several. In the embedded model, individual SREs or pairs join software engineering teams to apply automation, monitoring and incident response. Consulting teams instead advise organizations on adopting SRE practices.

sysd-reliab-185.title: Business impact analysis: what a disruption would cost
sysd-reliab-185.text: A business impact analysis identifies and evaluates the effects of disruptions on operations and determines the recovery priorities and strategies the organization needs. It identifies critical activities and their dependencies, and assesses the financial, operational, reputational and legal impact of disruption. For each function it assigns two objectives. The recovery point objective is the acceptable data loss, such as whether losing 2 days of data is acceptable. The recovery time objective is the acceptable time to restore the function. The longest that key services can be unavailable before stakeholders see unacceptable consequences is the maximum tolerable period of disruption.

sysd-reliab-186.title: Disaster recovery tiers: from no off-site data to automation
sysd-reliab-186.text: Disaster recovery tiers grade recovery solutions from no off-site data up to highly automated recovery. SHARE defined seven tiers in 1992, and IBM updated them to eight in 2012. Tier 0 has no off-site data or recovery plan, so recovery may be impossible. Higher tiers keep data fresher and recover faster. Tier 2 adds a hot site to restore tape backups. Tier 4 uses disk-based point-in-time copies. Tier 7 adds automated application recovery, which restores systems faster and more reliably than manual procedures.

sysd-reliab-215.title: Gmail restores user data from tape
sysd-reliab-215.text:
Gmail lost a significant amount of user data despite many safeguards, internal checks and redundancies. The loss went beyond what its internal recovery means could restore, so the team turned to GTape, Gmail's global offline tape backup. It was the first large-scale use of GTape to restore live customer data, though similar restores had been simulated many times.

Those simulations paid off. The team estimated how long the restore would take. It restored all accounts within several hours of the estimate, and recovered 99%+ of the data before the estimated completion time. The smooth recovery relied on a central plan, the product of regular dress rehearsals and dry runs, with many teams, even unrelated ones, pitching in.

The case shows {{ref:sysd-reliab-206}} at work. Backing up an online system gives defense in depth at two layers. One guards against failure of internal redundancy and backup subsystems. The other guards against a wide failure or zero-day in a device driver or filesystem under the disks. Large disk and network resources for replication did not remove the need for a tape layer, as {{ref:sysd-reliab-210}} explains. Multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism. Failures are treated as inevitable, so planning covers foreseeable failures and some amount of random, undifferentiated breakage as well.

sysd-reliab-216.title: Runaway deletion at Google Music
sysd-reliab-216.text:
A redesigned, more efficient data deletion pipeline wrongly removed about 600,000 audio references, affecting 21,000 users. The damage was found over a month after the pipeline's first run. The team disabled the pipeline, then split up. SREs recovered data from offsite tape while developers hunted the root cause, since recovery would be in vain until the bug was fixed.

The timing helped. The recovery came weeks after the annual disaster recovery testing exercise, so the tape team knew its subsystems' limits and had a tool tested in that exercise. Recovering the tracks meant recalling over 5,000 tapes, split into 5,475 restore jobs. SRE requested them programmatically, since a person typing one restore a minute would need over three days. The 1.5 petabyte first wave ran past its two-day estimate, with 17 bad tapes and 1,862 tapes a vendor omitted. Redundant encoding let the team recall redundancy tapes, and users had the tracks back in just short of 7 days.

About 161,000 tracks were deleted before being backed up. Store-bought and promotional ones were reinstated from original copies, while user-uploaded files were re-uploaded by clients over more than a week.

The root cause was a race condition. Stages designed to run in strict succession slowed as data grew, the timing assumption failed for more data, and wrong data was deleted nondeterministically. The pipeline was redesigned to remove the race. Monitoring was enhanced to catch runaway deletion bugs before users notice. One example is alerting when the global deletion rate crosses an extreme threshold such as 10x the 95th percentile.

reviews.service-levels-and-disaster-recovery: The measures in this chapter all answer one question: how much failure can a service afford? Indicators measure the service, objectives set the target and agreements put it in a contract, while an error budget turns the gap into room for risk. Recovery has its own pair of limits, the recovery point and recovery time objectives, and backups, standby sites and tiers are chosen to meet them. Protection works in layers, because replication is not backup, soft deletion catches developer error, and recovery that is never tested may be broken when it is needed. Monitoring, alerting and incident management tell people when the layers fail, and the Gmail and Google Music recoveries show those layers holding.
